title: Moving from Form to Formlessness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett emphasizes the importance of developing stability and insight through meditation practice, allowing us to see beyond our assumptions and theories about reality. This involves cultivating a sense of grounding and equanimity, as well as taking a fresh look at our understanding of the world. By exploring concepts such as formlessness and awareness, we can begin to see that everything is ephemeral and fabricated, leading to freedom from suffering and a more open way of living.

A little happier, a little kinder, a little more generous, or a lot.
But that alone is just our limited life.
So the practice is to help us feel a quality of the bigger than me, the bigger than self, the bigger than this limited-being aspect of our lives.
The unlimited quality of our living.
Anyway, I picked up this book by Rodney Smith, which somebody recommended to me, called *Touching the Infinite*.
Rodney Smith is a teacher not in this lineage, actually.
He's more in the Theravada, Vipassana lineages, connected to earliest Buddhism coming to us through Thailand and Burma and India.

But he's really reinterpreting it in a sort of Zen way, although he doesn't call it that.
In this book, instead of limited and unlimited, he speaks about form and formlessness: that we are so keyed into and oriented around form, so stuff.
And the most important stuff to us is this stuff, physical stuff, but also mental stuff.
It's all stuff, it's all form.
I want to read you a couple of excerpts from this book and make a few comments, because it's cogent with what I was trying to say last week.
By the way, Jeff Kelly and I explored these themes quite a lot at the recent Indianola sesshin, and the talks came out really quite well, I think, so you might find the recordings helpful.
There's a series of talks, and we trade off and build on each other in a really organic way.

And that's why all these great Dharma teachers can write so many books.
Do you know that?
They don't actually write them.
Their students transcribe their talks and do an initial edit, and then they polish it up a little bit.
I found out how he could have written a hundred books.
He didn't actually write them, but he gave those teachings.
Anyway, let me see, where did I want to start?
Okay, so here's Rodney Smith.
*As noted in the introduction, there are a number of terms the Buddha used for nirvana,*
so nirvana, the reputed goal of Buddhism, especially early Buddhism,
*one of which was the unmanifest or the formless.
The unmanifest or the formless.
The spiritual journey, as I will now frame it, is the movement from form to formless, which I will show is indistinguishable from the movement from suffering to its end.*
That's what the whole book is about: the spiritual journey is about being hung up in form, moving into something he's calling formlessness, and then a kind of reintegration of those things.
His main argument is that we usually focus Buddhism, especially this early Buddhist material, on suffering and the end of suffering.
But he's saying this idea of form and formlessness might be more helpful, because we don't like suffering so much, and we get a little tangled up the minute we start to think about it.
So he goes on.
*Initially, most of us understand form as the material world.
In its grand display, form is the universe we witness through our senses.
And in its most subtle manifestations, it is the wisp of a thought or an image that passes through consciousness.*
So a thought is also a form.
*Form covers all experiences and appearances and has the quality of standing outside of and in isolation from everything else.
Form covers all experiences and appearances and has a quality of standing outside of and in isolation from everything else.*
So form is very separated.
*This is true of all formations, including the sense of our own existence.
We feel as if we are a separately formed existence from anything else observed or known.
Once objects are in contrast to one another, they have edges that rub against other objects, creating friction and conflict, resulting in suffering.*
We all know about this.
*The edges are more than the physical limits of the objects.
They include the personal and psychological boundaries of our opinions, our values, our comfort range, our areas of ownership and possession.
When the world is formed into separate objects, our boundaries inhibit further communion and interconnection.
And we become inaccessible and isolated.
This is the first manifestation of suffering.
And it's rarely noted as a problem, since separation, in our usual worldview, is just a fact.
But as our perception begins to be spiritually altered, we notice that we are both separated from the world and at the same time there's a deeper level of interconnection.
But it's not being lived yet.
Somehow this intrinsic connectedness is rarely acknowledged within consensus reality, but it's unmistakable as our thoughts quiet down.
We sense a union that [unclear: "bellies"] the profusion of discrete objects that we see.*
Is this making sense?
Consensus reality is everything separate.
It's all about form.
But as we practice we start to feel that there's something bigger than that.
This is what I was saying last week about our unlimited life.
And every culture has some way of describing this, right?
God, spirituality, whatever you want to call it.
The universe.
That's a little more from Rodney.
*So the first part of the spiritual journey is moving from a world in which form is the predominant way of relating to life and desiring and avoiding form.*
Wait, let me start over here.
I'm confused.
*The first part of the spiritual journey is moving from a world in which form is the predominant way of relating to life and desiring and avoiding form, the primary way we navigate through life.
Going from that to the formless paradigm that is both immaterial and unified.
The formless is the sacred.
Formless is the sacred.
And has been called awareness in some traditions and the Holy Ghost in others.
Awareness is a Holy Ghost in the sense that it's invisible and lies beneath the ability of our minds to isolate it.
If it were visible, it would be just another expression of form.
Awareness is empty of thingness,*
put that in quotes.
*Awareness is undifferentiated, yet awareness embraces all expressions of form and is therefore free of conflict and suffering.*
He's talking about awareness.
We can manifest awareness, we can practice awareness, and awareness can be with form, but it's not form.
Then he's got a little thought experiment, so let's try it.
Or actually, a perception experiment.
*Quiet yourself.*
I'm going to sit in here all evening quietly, so hopefully you're somewhat quiet.
*Quiet yourself and focus on the forms in front of you.*
Let's actually do this.
*Focus on the forms in front of you.*
Maybe I'm the form in front of you.
I'm just a form to you.
*Listen to what the mind says about each form you see.
The mind likely knows what each object is and has a name for it.
Perhaps its history.
The mind sees things as pleasant or unpleasant.
The mind sees shape and color.*
Is that true?
*This is form consciousness or object consciousness.
We see things as separate, discrete things with all these qualities.
Now, relax your eyes and do not focus specifically on any object.
Let your gaze be really soft and sense the alive space, sense the space within which each form appears.
Sense and feel the space in which form appears.
Let this alive space surround and hold the objects you see.
If you have relaxed [unclear: "efficiently"], you may sense that space encompasses a sense of aliveness, that there's something fuller and richer than the mere sight of an object.
This is awareness of formlessness.
Though the formlessness cannot be experienced, it can be sensed.*
I'd say it can be felt.
*Learn to differentiate between form and the formless.*
So that's an interesting practice, not just to do once, and it's tricky because I'm talking to you.
But as you go around your day, notice the way habitually and instantly we divvy things up into forms, and we hardly even notice them either, right?
We just put names on them and keep moving because we've got stuff to do.
But try to stop and have a soft gaze, or soft ears, actually.
Let's see if you can notice and feel the space, the formlessness from which form arises.
What he's suggesting in this book, and I really agree with him, is that this is a path to less suffering.
This isn't just a metaphysical thing or a weird experiment.
To feel and sense and connect with the formless is to connect and open to our unlimited life, our bigger life.
Suzuki Roshi calls it big mind, our big mind.
And we're not all hung up in forms.
We're more flexible.
We're more open.
We're less defended.
And here are a few more pages from Rodney when he talks about that.
The first one was from the introductory chapter, and this part is from the chapter on mindfulness of the mind, the third foundation of mindfulness.
Let's listen a little more for Rodney, and then I'll make a few more comments.
*Most of us believe that by living as a separate entity within the world of form, the essential answers to our existence will eventually be disclosed.
Answers to questions like who are we, what life is, where does our happiness lie, and what is our ultimate purpose and meaning.*
So we believe that living as a separate entity in the world of form eventually will figure all this out.
*We keep trying to discover these key answers within the individuated objects, situations, and circumstances that actually keep us bound.
Focusing on form, focusing on formations ties us to their limitations.
And as we attempt to answer our existential questions, the forms of the world are arising and passing away in front of our eyes.
The problem is that we do not know how to stop focusing only on form.*
We're just caught up in form.
*Feeling lost, we just keep maintaining the same direction, gazing out upon the world of objects, hoping that we have inadvertently missed something.
We just look again and look harder.
The solutions are out there and attainable.
We just need to keep looking.
The heart of what the Buddha is saying is to look and see if we have missed something.
As long as we stare in the same direction towards form, we will get the same results, suffering and separation.
So the Buddha suggests a variety of ways in this text and otherwise.
The Buddha suggests a variety of ways to disenchant us from investing in form.
To disenchant us from investing in form.
He shows us that everything is ephemeral and everything is going to die.
It's not worth our involvement when form continually slides through our fingers.
This too shall pass and that shall fade away and that and that.
He's saying that the world is mind created and that it is all coming from us.
And it's a total fabrication.
We fabricate form.
We're telling the story of the world, mentally making it into something, and grasping after our own creation.
And of course, we're in the middle.

In addition, Buddha is saying that feelings, pleasant, neutral, unpleasant feelings, the feelings we have for objects, the attraction and aversion we have for objects, are actually just coming from us.
That the object itself is without value and we have assigned its worth.
Stay long enough with any object and our feelings about it will change.
Finally, he points back to our sense of self, our very sense of our self, and asks whether we have any more substance than the other objects that we create in our minds.
He's attempting to bring us to the inevitable conclusion that all is empty.
From subject to object, from mind to body, all experiences, all forms, all types of consciousness is all empty.
And all our boundaries are self-imposed and without merit.
There is nothing to our body and there is no mind that analyzes and systematizes experience.
We are not what we think we are and our suffering is directly related to believing what our thoughts say.

So these are pretty strong statements.
Everything's just in our mind.
Is that really true?
I think it's really worth bringing this up in your daily life and spending some time with this.
And of course the mind that does all this, if what he's saying is true, is going to be a little resistant to this kind of teaching.
It would be surprising if your mind didn't argue with this, because this is saying that your mind's all wrong.
All wrong in its basic assumptions about who and what we are.
Not only is it wrong, it's causing our suffering.
We would not like to blame our suffering on ourselves particularly.
We would like it to be something else.
At the very least, something that we can fix within the usual parameters that we're comfortable with.
So these kinds of teachings are inherently uncomfortable in a certain way.
They're uncomfortable to this limited self, to the self that only is hanging out in the world of form.
But the good news is, as we take this kind of thing in and practice with it, meditate with it with stability and curiosity, we can also feel a great sense of relief gradually seeping in.
What a relief it would be if we didn't have to defend our opinions and our views and our personal time.
What a relief it would be if we didn't have to fix everything.

What a relief it would be if there's a quality of life that is uncreated, and that means it doesn't need to be fixed, doesn't need to be attended to, and can just be trusted and held by and immersed in.
So these teachings can be a great path to freedom and less suffering.
You know, the Buddha was not just saying less suffering either.
That's really understating the case.
He was saying freedom from suffering, freedom from suffering, free in suffering.
So I just really want to encourage all of us to muse about this, turn it over.
You might find this particular book helpful, but there's a million other books and a million other teachings.
Someone was asking me the other day about the Heart Sutra, in the very reasonable, what-the-heck kind of way that we chanted this evening, that part about no eyes, no ears, no nose.
It's about this, actually.
It's basically saying that the reality you think you're taking in with your eyes is not that reality.
That's what they mean by no eyes.
The sounds that you hear, that you take to be a certain quality of experience, are not that.
So there's no ears.
It's easy to misunderstand this kind of material, easy for it to sound like, well, are you saying there's no problems?
There are very real problems in the world.
People are suffering.
So it doesn't mean that.

What it means is, if we can practice in a way that we have some felt sense, available to us, of this formlessness of our unlimited life, we're more able to act skillfully within the world of form, because we're not so caught up in just a certain way.
We're not as caught up in our reactions to it, because we can see it's just one half of the equation.
It's not the whole reality.
It's important and it matters.
And he comes off a little strong.
It's good to have teachers that come across a little strong to shake us up.
I don't know if I'd really talk the way Rodney Smith does, but I appreciate what he's saying a lot because it's helping me to study this.
Because our connection to the formlessness allows us to be gentle in the world of form, because it's only one thing.
It's just one part of it.
Does that make any sense?
Or is it making useful nonsense?
Useful nonsense.
Useful nonsense.
Does anyone have anything they'd like to say or ask or add?
I actually am following the directions of my advisory council and I only talked for 25 minutes.
I'm proud of myself.
I just like that.
**Participant:** What's the name of the book again?
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** It's called *Touching the Infinite, A New Perspective on the Buddha's Four Foundations of Mindfulness*.
He's quite different in the way he talks about the sutra than his colleagues in the Vipassana world.
I don't know what they think of him, but I appreciate him.
And our founding teacher, Norman Fischer, who's a great, what do they call it?
The little squib on the back?
**Participant:** Blurb.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** He's a great blurber, so he has a blurb on this.
One of these days I'll ask him if he actually read the whole book.
So he has a nice blurb.
Yeah, right, exactly.
Sometimes this connection with formlessness can appear as a dramatic experience.
Many of us have had interesting, illuminating experiences where it's like, wow.
But then sometimes the tradition sounds like it's all about that, and that's not really right either.
This tradition can sound like a driving quest, especially of this [unclear: "end"] tradition, to have some big experience of formlessness.
And some of us just aren't wired up that way.
We don't have a big experience of formlessness.
It's more that gradually we hold things a little more lightly.
The forms seem a little less urgent and intense and important, although they always are important.
So that's one thing that's easy to misunderstand about this kind of talking.
Like, oh, I should get it.
People come to the interviews and they say, I don't get it.
Well, that's trying to make the formless into a form anyway.
There's nothing to get.
And it's really important that we learn to non-get it and play with non-getting as well as with getting.
So we don't just make ourselves suffer more by turning this incredible tradition, which has this very subtle quality to it, subtle sense to it, into just another form, right?
Because that would diminish it and reduce its ability to heal.
You know what I'm saying?
Okay, maybe that's enough.
Thank you for listening.
*May our intentions equally extend to every [unclear: "meaning and place with the true merit buddhas"].*
